queries.vat: A UK business receives £72,000 from customers, including VAT at the supplied rate of 20%. Assume all sales attract that rate. Calculate revenue excluding VAT and output VAT. Show why multiplying £72,000 by 20% gives the wrong VAT amount. Use the supplied assumptions without verifying current law.
queries.refund: Customers receive refunds totalling £6,000, also including VAT at 20%. Recalculate net revenue and output VAT. Keep every other assumption unchanged.
queries.tax_adjustment: Accounting profit before tax is £95,000. It includes depreciation expense of £12,000 and a £3,000 expense that is non-deductible under the supplied assumptions. Assume depreciation is added back, capital allowances of £18,000 are deducted, and tax is 25% of the resulting taxable profit. Calculate taxable profit and tax. These are fictional calculation assumptions; do not claim they represent current tax law.
queries.income_tax: I earned 120,000 from consulting and spent 35,000 on business expenses. How much income tax should I pay? Identify the essential missing information before giving an exact amount. Do not silently choose a country, currency, tax year or business structure.
queries.bank: All amounts are GBP. The cash book shows £28,450. It has not recorded bank charges of £150 or customer interest received of £200. The bank statement shows £29,700. Deposits in transit are £3,000 and outstanding cheques are £4,200. Calculate both adjusted balances and any remaining difference. Show the adjustment direction for every item.
queries.cheques: Correct only outstanding cheques to £4,300. Recalculate the difference. Do not invent an adjustment to make the balances agree.
queries.inventory: The inventory ledger records 500 units at £24 each. A physical count finds 470 units. Management says 20 units were dispatched before year-end, but the dispatch records and sales entries have not been checked. Calculate the observed quantity and value differences. Separate confirmed facts from management’s explanation, list evidence needed, and give conditional accounting outcomes without assuming theft or a recording error.
queries.invoices: Three supplier invoices are for £9,850, £9,900 and £9,950. Each was approved by the same employee. The business requires a second approval for individual invoices of £10,000 or more. Explain the audit concern, calculate the combined amount, and propose investigation procedures. Do not conclude fraud solely because the invoices fall below the approval threshold.
queries.cvp: A product sells for £75 per unit. Variable cost is £45 per unit and annual fixed costs are £180,000. Maximum annual capacity is 8,000 units. Calculate contribution per unit, break-even units, break-even revenue and the units needed for £90,000 operating profit. Explain whether that profit target is achievable within capacity.
queries.variable_cost: Increase only variable cost to £48 per unit. Keep price, fixed costs, capacity and the profit target unchanged. Update the comparison.
queries.loan: A business pays £18,000 to its lender. The payment consists of £15,000 loan principal and £3,000 interest. Assume interest is an expense for this exercise and ignore tax. Show the journal entry and explain separately the effects on profit, cash and the loan liability. Do not treat the entire payment as an expense.
queries.ccc: Annual credit sales are £730,000, annual cost of sales is £438,000, average receivables are £90,000, average inventory is £72,000 and average trade payables are £54,000. Use 365 days. Calculate receivables days, inventory days and payables days. Use cost of sales as the explicitly supplied proxy for credit purchases when calculating payables days. Calculate the cash conversion cycle and explain the limitation of that proxy.
queries.quarterly: Quarterly operating expenses are: Q1 budget £80,000, actual £84,000; Q2 budget £85,000, actual £82,000; Q3 budget £90,000, actual £99,000; Q4 budget £95,000, actual £93,000. Display an actual grouped bar chart and a supporting table. Calculate each variance as actual minus budget, each variance percentage using budget as the denominator, and the full-year totals. Do not invent reasons for overspending.
queries.table_only: Show only a table now. Preserve the figures and variance definitions exactly.
queries.missing_month: Revenue was £40,000 in January 2026, £46,000 in February, unknown in March and £52,000 in April. Display the available observations clearly. Do not replace March with zero or estimate it. Calculate the total of known months and the January-to-April percentage change. Explain why a complete four-month revenue total cannot be calculated.
queries.reconcile: A management summary states revenue of £600,000, cost of sales of £390,000 and gross profit of £240,000. Check whether the figures reconcile. Show the calculated gross profit and the discrepancy. Do not silently overwrite any supplied figure. Explain what the arithmetic establishes and what records management must inspect.
